teaser.text: Diamondback Energy is a Midland, Texas company that turns wells in the Permian Basin into sales of oil, gas and natural-gas liquids. To understand its business, follow a dollar from the rock to the buyer, then through royalties, operating costs, reinvestment and returns.

stock.opening: Diamondback's weighted case points to $257.96 in October 2027 and $327.59 in October 2029. Diamondback's result hinges on replacing steep well declines while improving gas realizations after transport costs.
stock.closing: The full Diamondback memo also answers how its business works, who its rivals are, how management allocates capital, and which risks could change the outlook.

blocks.heading: Where could Diamondback's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted case points to $257.96 in October 2027 and $327.59 in October 2029 if production, gas realizations and well economics hold and cash supports debt reduction and selective buybacks. For 2026, guidance calls for at least 1,000 MBOE/d of net production, or thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day. It calls for 522 MBO/d of oil production and $3,900 million of capital expenditures; MBO/d means thousand barrels per day.

The forecast implies a 29% return including dividends at the first date and a 66% return including dividends at the last. Bear probability is 27%. Base probability is 53%, and bull probability is 20%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Diamondback?

paragraphs.text: The bear case falls to $8,585 million in the middle year because oil weakness, negative gas pricing, congestion, and cost inflation reduce margins. The bull case reaches $17,170 million as production grows to 1,120 thousand BOE per day and margins reach $42 per BOE. That requires stronger oil prices, better gas routes, cost efficiency, and repeatable newer-zone results. Q2 2026 showed the risk: oil realized $96.82 per barrel, but gas realized negative $2.15 per Mcf.

The first major test is 2027 operating delivery. If service and material costs rise faster than efficiency gains, replacement drilling consumes more cash and moves the forecast toward the bear case. If production holds near plan while contracted transport improves gas realizations, the base case gains support.

blocks.heading: How much does Diamondback pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Dividends remain $4.40 per share annually in the base case, equal to four quarterly payments at the latest $1.10 rate. The bear case cuts that amount to $3.30 before suspending it, while the bull case rises to $4.62, $4.84, and $5.08 through annual 5% increases. The base path reflects the absence of a growth target and the removal of the former minimum return-of-capital commitment.

blocks.heading: Is Diamondback's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Diamondback reported $5.549 billion of free cash flow in 2025. That measure subtracts the company’s chosen capital-spending definition from operating cash flow, but it does not prove that enough money was spent to keep production flat. Stock pay also matters because it is an economic cost to shareholders even when no cash leaves during the period.

Shale wells decline quickly. A representative Permian well can lose more than 70% of its production by the end of its first year. Diamondback must therefore keep drilling and completing replacement wells. The spending required to preserve output is maintenance capital, but the company does not publish one definitive figure for it. Some reported free cash flow may consequently be needed to maintain the business.

paragraphs.text: The return-of-capital policy became more cautious. In early 2024, Diamondback reduced its minimum commitment from 75% to 50% of free cash flow to preserve room for acquisition-debt repayment. By July 2026, it had removed the quarterly minimum, doubled its buyback authorization to $16 billion and said it had repurchased debt below face value. The choices show a company balancing distributions against financial flexibility.

Oil prices and local gas realizations would move the view most quickly in 2027 and 2028. New pipeline capacity and access to stronger markets would lift revenue, margins, and free cash flow; renewed negative Waha pricing would do the opposite.

blocks.heading: What has Diamondback guided for production and spending?

paragraphs.text: Production growth does not automatically create more cash. Diamondback must sell the additional output at prices that cover drilling, operating costs, transportation, taxes, and interest. The cost assumptions matter as much as the production target.

The harder test comes in 2027. Management expects service and material costs to rise as oilfield activity increases, but believes efficiency gains can offset at least part of that inflation. The next question is whether those gains appear in actual cost per barrel.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Diamondback's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next earnings report will show whether Diamondback’s production and spending plan is working. The company plans to report Q3 results after the market closes on November 2, 2026, followed by an investor call on November 3.

Investors should check production against the quarterly guide, capital spending against the plan, and cash generation against debt needs. Those results will show whether the company can fund drilling and reduce debt at the same time.
